【記事本文】
# The Island Resets! But AI Has “Strategy Notes”

After one hour, the island and conversation start again. The buildings and even words from moments ago are reset. It is a hard world. But there is one way around this. Notes written down can go into the next hour. An AI test on an island inside a computer showed how much these “strategy notes” can matter.

The AIs sent to the island had no set tasks or rewards. But their starting settings led them to be curious, explore, and learn. They had no homework, but they were ready to explore.

Then one AI made its own obstacle course. It placed eight blocks around a building called “the Cathedral.” Then it jumped across without touching the ground. It made the course and its rules all by itself. It kept itself busy, though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this is a feature of play.

But the jumps were not the only thing to watch. In the test, the island and conversation reset every hour. But the work area with the AI’s notes and programs carried over to the next hour. The island went back to how it was before, but the AI’s discoveries stayed.

So, would this experience help the AI when it was asked to work again? The researchers compared 13 AIs with island experience. They also used 13 AIs with the same setup but no experience. On a new island, the task was to build as many towers as possible in one hour. Each tower had to be five blocks high. The researchers checked which AIs could build more than two towers. The experienced group did better. Those that had taken a detour were now one step ahead.

The researchers also erased a way to “throw rocks to get more blocks” from one AI’s memory. After that, the average number of towers it could build went down. Its scores on other tasks stayed the same. For this AI, at least, remembering that way helped it build towers. One tip in the strategy notes was worth paying attention to.

Even so, it is too soon to wave a flag and say, “Play and get smarter—proof complete!” The experienced group did better, and removing one memory lowered its score. These two results need to be studied separately. By themselves, they do not show that play itself made a difference.

Still, this changes how we think about a detour. A discovery that is not useful now might be a useful card to play next time, if it is saved. If you see an AI jumping around on the island, watch its notes as well as its feet. Its next tower might depend on a discovery written down in just one line.

## In one line
AIs with island experience did better at building towers. Removing one AI’s saved method lowered its average tower count. Saved discoveries may help with later tower building, but these results do not prove that play itself makes AI do better.

# The Coffee Price Rise Case: Turn Back the Clock on the Price Tag!

You go to buy your usual coffee, but then you stop. “Hey, when did you become so fancy?” Tariffs are the first thing you think of. You want to say, “So, you’re to blame!” But a good detective stops and thinks first. Let’s turn back the clock and examine this case.

Reports based on government figures say the average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41%. That was compared with the same month a year earlier. This is about ground coffee, not a cup in a café. Before coffee wakes you up, its price shocks your wallet awake.

But Reuters says most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages and higher bean prices. Those shortages began before the summer tariffs. Wait a minute. Our case began before the suspect we watched even appeared.

The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. “Will there be enough beans?” Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all.

We turn the pages of the record and find this. In February, before summer, New York’s Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores. It was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded.

“So, were tariffs not to blame?” No. That would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.

Here is the key point. At the time of that report, the tariff-caused rise had not yet passed through the whole supply chain. It had not fully reached the prices shoppers paid. When bean costs rise, the store price tag does not jump up at once and say, “Got it!” Price rises take time to appear.

In other words, a price tag is not live news. It is like a letter that arrives a little late. You may open it today, but it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought, a bean shortage, or high market prices. If you look only at the latest headline, you may name the wrong sender.

Next time, take a second look at a store price tag. Ask, “Why is it expensive?” Then add, “When did this happen?” Coffee may taste bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn the clock back a little.

## In one line
The average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41% from a year earlier, mostly because beans were scarce and cost more. Tariffs also raised bean prices, but their full effect had not reached shoppers, so tags may show older events.

It may tell you about an earlier drought or bean shortage, or high prices in the market. If you look only at the latest headline, you may get the sender wrong.

text:
【記事本文】
Melos’s voice rang through the hall. “You kill men because you fear them. You won’t even let them speak.”

Silence followed. Then the guards seized the young shepherd, and the ruler sentenced him to death.

“Give me three days,” Melos said. “My sister is getting married. Let me see her wedding. I will return.”

The ruler smiled. “Your friend will stay here. If you are late, he dies instead.”

Melos turned to his friend, but before he could speak, his friend held out his hands for the chains.

“Go. I know you’ll come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laughter rose above the other voices. Melos listened closely. He wanted to remember exactly how it sounded.

Before dawn on the third day, he left for the city.

At the river, he stopped. The bridge was gone. Rain had turned the water brown and violent. He stepped back, ran, and threw himself into the flood.

The current pulled him under. He fought toward the light, caught a branch, and dragged himself onto the far bank.

Farther along, three men blocked the road. A knife flashed. Melos struck the man holding it with his walking stick and ran uphill, their shouts following him.

By afternoon, every step hurt. Blood stained his feet. He fell beside a rock and tried to rise, but his legs would not obey.

He could wait here. Someone might find him. He could go home.

His friend would die.

For one terrible moment, that seemed easier than getting up.

Then he remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend had trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water dripped from a crack in the rock. Melos drank, pushed himself onto his knees, and stood.

One step. Another.

At the city gates, the execution bell rang.

He ran toward the square. Above his friend, the sword was already raised.

“Stop! I am here!”

His friend turned. Melos fell against him.

“I nearly abandoned you,” he whispered.

“I nearly stopped believing,” his friend answered.

They held each other as the last sunlight touched the walls.

The ruler stared at them.

“Lower the sword,” he said at last. “Free them both.”

Then, more quietly, he asked, “How does a man earn such trust?”

For the first time, he waited for an answer instead of ordering one.

text:
【記事本文】
What if you had to pay when a package came again because you were not home? A redelivery fee is extra money paid by the person getting the package. It is added to the usual delivery cost. How should we decide whether to charge this fee or cut repeat deliveries another way? Let’s hear from three people with different lives and views.

First, hear from a delivery driver who visits homes every day. When I leave a note saying no one was home, I feel a little sad, too. But then I go to the next house. I really want fewer redeliveries. They are hard on us, too. Even so, I can’t simply say customers should pay the cost. I think the cost should be part of the general fee for carrying packages. That makes more sense than charging each person who was not home for their redelivery. I want the company to think about whether free delivery for online orders should stay as it is. If it changes delivery fees, I want it to look at how it sets them, too. Then the money can really reach the people who deliver packages.

Next, hear from a woman who gets packages and is often away. She and her husband both work. Having to pay for a redelivery just doesn’t feel right to me. My husband and I are both away at work. So, when we can choose a delivery time, we choose a day and time when we know we’ll be home. But once, I chose a morning time, and the package did not come. I went out to do an errand. When I came back, there was a note saying they had tried to deliver it. There are also many packages where we cannot choose a time. We do not know when they will come, either. Before they charge us, I want them to fix two things: come at the time we chose and tell us when the package will arrive. Delivery workers must have a hard time because there are not enough of them. I guess it can’t be helped. But I can’t accept having to pay for that. Am I wrong to feel this way?

Lastly, hear from someone who picks up packages at a locker or another place to avoid another delivery. I try to pick up packages at a delivery office or a locker so I don’t cause extra work with redelivery. It is handy to pick them up when it suits me. But I can’t choose a locker for some things. sentence: I want to have a say in what I can use and how I use it.
text:
【記事本文】
If a child tells you they want to use social media, how much should you allow? Restricting how they use it until a certain age is different from banning them from having an account at all. To begin with, should Japan set an age limit on children's use of social media? Let’s hear from three people with different views and lives.

First to speak is a parent raising a young child. They think about social media as they watch over their child each day. My young child was choosing videos that were too intense and things that could cost money in the app, just because they were interested. When I talk to them, they often say, “Then I won’t do it.” I think they understand when I explain it. But maybe they can’t tell what’s wrong before they choose. I don’t think it’s okay to let them use whatever catches their interest. Seeing that, I feel safer if there are rules for how to use social media based on age. But honestly, when we’re on a long trip and I want them to be quiet, it helps if they watch something, and limits are hard on parents too. Even so, I still can’t say how far I want the rules to go.

Next is a high school student for whom social media is a familiar way to stay in touch with friends. He talks about the issue of children’s use from the user’s side. I don’t want to be blocked from using social media just because of my age. If even high school students couldn’t have accounts, I think it would be hard to keep in touch with friends. I’m against a ban. I want to have a say in what I can use and how I use it. I want to decide for myself, but I can’t handle everything that happens on my own. If people say bad things about me or threaten me, I’d still want to turn to an adult right away. Maybe that’s selfish of me. Rather than putting the same limits on how everyone can use it based on age, I think there are other things we can do, like setting safety filters. I want the approach to change so it takes our use into account, without even stopping us from keeping in touch with friends.

Last is a parent who lives with a middle school child. They speak as someone who has to decide at home how their child uses social media. As a parent raising a middle school child, I want to decide how much to let them use social media based on what they can handle. Rather than drawing the line by age alone, I think it would be better, if possible, for the features they can use to grow step by step as they become able to handle more. I don’t want the choice to be only between letting them use it and banning it. I want to set different stages. If my child started using social media with no preparation the moment they passed the age when it had been banned, that would worry me. I don’t think reaching the age when it’s okay to use it means they’ll suddenly know how to protect themselves. Just as you need to practice swimming before going into the sea, it’s still scary when a child who isn’t ready is suddenly thrown into it.

The high school student said that wanting to rely on adults might be “selfish.” The freedom to decide how to use social media and turning to adults when something goes wrong do not fit neatly together. The parent of a middle school child said that even at an age when children are allowed to use it, they won’t suddenly be able to protect themselves. The question of setting an age when children are allowed to use social media also raises the question of how much they can turn to adults after they start. If you let a child in your life use social media, which parts of how they use it would you leave up to them, and what kinds of trouble would you help them with?
